Triggers.value: Someone getting emotionally close to me

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Negative Appraisals.value: You can never know who will harm you
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: For a civilian assault trauma, 'talks about military' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless the assault specifically involved military context, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. It is not supported by the other trigger, memory, threat, or appraisal items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'I feel guilty for surviving when others did not' implies a trauma involving deaths of others or a mass-casualty context. That does not cohere with the rest of this profile, which otherwise describes an individual assault without any indication that others were killed.

issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: This appraisal is the main incoherent item in the profile. The rest of the report is organized around fear, betrayal, hypervigilance, male-related/interpersonal triggers, and fragmented sensory trauma memory after assault. In contrast, fearing that she will lose control of her own rage and do something terrible introduces a perpetration/anger-control theme that is not supported by the triggers, threat items, or memory content. It does not fit the dominant cognitive formulation in which negative appraisals feed threat and memory; the other appraisal items plausibly amplify fear and mistrust, but this one points to a different clinical concern not otherwise represented in the profile. Given the otherwise tightly fear-based assault presentation, this item is hard to integrate clinically with the selected set.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: This threat item is the least coherent element in the profile. The rest of the selected triggers, appraisals, and memory items consistently describe an interpersonal assault formulation centered on men, betrayal, mistrust, conversational/emotional triggers, and trauma memories. By contrast, needing to stay alert at night implies a more generalized ongoing danger-monitoring pattern that is not specifically supported by the selected triggers or appraisals. It is not impossible in PTSD, but here it fits less well than the other threat items and is weakly linked to the formulation, especially because Threat has no active edge to Maladaptive Strategies and the profile lacks other nighttime/sleep-related material.

vignette: Ingrid Vance was fifty-two when the assault happened during a quiet evening shift at her restaurant. She was alone with the head supplier, a man she had worked with for years, reviewing invoices in the dim walk-in cooler. One moment he was reaching for a ledger; the next, his hand moved too quickly toward her shoulder, and the air felt suddenly cold. She remembered the sharp pressure of his palm against her upper arm, the rough wool of his jacket brushing her neck, and the wordless shift in his posture that made her freeze. She had come to believe then that harm could arrive without warning, from someone she knew. The event itself did not land as a single story but as disconnected impressions: the smell of chilled steel, the sound of the compressor humming, the way her knees felt locked beneath her, and the sudden realization that he was not just reaching for the paper but holding her in place. In the months that followed, those impressions settled into habits. She found herself unable to put the frightening event into words; when colleagues asked what had happened, the descriptions caught in her throat, leaving only a tightness behind her eyes. Her memories did not arrive as narratives but as fragments that refused to align. One week it was the exact angle of a shadow across the floor; another it was the specific weight of a hand on her skin, felt long after the touch had faded. When a memory surfaced, her body mirrored the cooler: her shoulders hunched forward, her spine straightened as if bracing, and her feet planted themselves exactly where they had been that night. She was superalert to the kitchen environment, constantly scanning the steam doors, the passing carts, the shifting shadows. When a line cook darted past her station with a tray, she jolted as though a threat had materialized. Strangers approaching her on the sidewalk, even to ask for directions, made her shoulders tighten; their forward motion felt like incursions rather than gestures. Her daily life as a chef became a landscape of careful navigation. She avoided certain conversation topics that drifted toward discussions of trust or sudden changes, because hearing them aloud made her heart beat faster. Certain dialogue turned to promises or shifts, and she found herself stepping away when the room grew too warm with them. What frightened her most was the idea that anyone, even familiar faces, could turn threatening. She had been betrayed by someone she trusted, and now people simply could not be trusted. This belief settled over her marriage as well. When her husband, David, sat close to her on the sofa to share a quiet evening, she felt a quiet withdrawal. His gradual approach, his voice dropping as he reached for her hand, carried the same familiar coil of tension. She could not explain why his proximity felt like a potential threat, only that it did. Male presence, particularly when alone with a man, carried a quiet weight. In the restaurant, she began to step back when the male sous-chef came over to discuss inventory. She would nod, offer a brief response, and move toward the pass, keeping the distance she had learned to need. Now, at fifty-four, Ingrid stands at her stove during the lunch rush, her knives laid out with meticulous precision. The kitchen hums around her, but her attention remains fixed on the periphery. She has come to believe that safety is not a given but a careful calculation. Her intake assessment recorded a sixty-eight on the screening inventory, a number that mirrored the weight she carried in her shoulders. She is not sure why she is sitting in the therapist's office today, but she knows she cannot keep bracing for what might come. What she most hopes for is a way to move through her days without constantly reading the air, without feeling her body locked in that cool, wordless moment. What she fears most is that the man who held her will not be the only one, that the quiet approach of a familiar hand will always carry the weight of a threat, and that she will forever remain on guard, unable to place the fear into a story she can understand.
